transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-06
Start time: 14:30 PST
Duration: ~46m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood SRE), Priya Singh (NimbusRx ML), Owen McCarthy (NimbusRx Platform), Rita Alvarez (Product), Jon (CTO, joined at 00:12)

Summary:
Quick sync on pilot throughput numbers from last 48h, tuning continuous batching and concurrency settings, investigating queue jitter seen at spike windows, agree next steps for bench+traces.

Topics discussed:
- Recent pilot runs and steady-state vs cold-start behavior
- Effect of continuous batching window + max_batch_size on latency/cost
- Concurrency targets vs queue depth and backpressure
- KV cache thrash on multi-tenant model variants
- Fallbacks to quantized model for tail latency cost control
- Security/legal ask and next demo/runbook handoff

Action items recap (short): see action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): All right, folks, thanks for joining. We have about 45 minutes, quick agenda — numbers from the 48-hour run, tuning suggestions, and assign next steps.
[00:12] Jon (NimbusRx): Hey sorry I popped in late, had a quick exec check-in, should be here for the handoff.
[00:18] Devon (Redwood): No worries. I want to start with Slide 1 — the 2-day baseline. We saw a steady-state throughput of ~820 rps at 80 concurrent workers, mean tokens per request ~210, avg seq len around 230, p50 generation latency 78ms, p95 at 210ms, p99 spikes to 640ms during burst windows.
[00:35] Priya (NimbusRx): Wait you said 820 rps at 80 conc, that's the test harness number right? On our prod-like traffic the user flows have a bimodal length: quick auth summarizers ~40 tokens and long note summaries ~1,100 tokens. So the average is skewed, I think we saw more tail in our internal metrics.
[00:55] Devon (Redwood): Yeah the harness mixes slices but good call — we split traffic into 60/40 short vs long in the bench. The p99 spikes correlate to when the long flows hit a cold KV cache; there's a rebuild cost.
[01:08] Owen (NimbusRx): To be clear, the cold KV cache is per-GPU, right? We observed cross-replica cache misses after autoscaling events which matches that.
[01:18] Samir (Redwood): Correct, cache is per-worker. Autoscale or replica reassignments cause cold prefixes. We're seeing KV eviction thrash in the 30-90s window which surfaces at p99.
[01:30] Priya: Can you define thrash there? We're seeing occasional 1–2 second tails which kill our SLO.
[01:36] Samir: By thrash I mean frequent eviction+reload of KV keys; if many long sequences get interleaved without sticky routing the cache doesn't warm. There's also a small mismatch between our batching window and your burst shape.
[01:52] Rita (NimbusRx): You mentioned batching window — are you leaning shorter or longer? Our product team wants latency to feel instant for short queries.
[02:02] Devon: Right, so continuous batching has two knobs we tuned: max_batch_size and batching latency window (ms). In recent runs we used max_batch_size 64 and window 30ms. That gave better throughput but increased short-query p50 slightly due to grouping. For short-query dominated routes we recommend reducing window to 8–12ms and lowering max_batch_size to 16.
[02:25] Priya: Hmm that sounds like it will lower throughput. Any rule-of-thumb tradeoff?
[02:29] Devon: Roughly, smaller window+batch reduces per-request latency but increases token cost per inference headroom — throughput may drop ~12–18% for same GPU pool. But you won't see the 200ms p50 bump.
[02:40] Owen: Is there an automatic hybrid mode? I recall Redwood has routing by route or per-path policies.
[02:46] Maya: Yep — you can pin routes. For auth summary flows we can set dedicated low-latency route with small window; long-form summarizers can be on a high-throughput route with larger batch. That preserves UX for short queries while keeping cost down.
[02:59] Jon: That makes sense. But how about concurrency targets and queueing? We're seeing queue depth oscillate.
[03:06] Samir: The pilot cluster uses a per-replica request queue with a soft limit. When concurrency is bumped to maintain throughput, queue depth can back up if the batcher waits to fill batches. Two levers: increase concurrency but reduce batch window, or add rate-shaping upstream to smooth burst arrival.
[03:23] Priya: Could we try adjusting concurrency targets? We currently target 80 coroutines/threads per GPU, that value came from initial sizing.
[03:31] Devon: We recommend targeting concurrency in the 60–100 range depending on sequence-length mix. For your token mix, I'd propose testing 95 concurrency with max_batch_size 48 and window 20ms — that should flatten throughput but reduce p99 spikes by avoiding queue pileup.
[03:49] Priya: Okay let's put that in the 2-hour benchmark.
[03:53] Owen: Curious — what about cost? If we increase concurrency to 95 and slightly larger batches, do we hit lower per-token cost or higher?
[04:02] Devon: Larger batches reduce per-token compute overhead, so unit cost goes down, but increasing concurrency can raise active replica counts briefly if autoscale reacts to push. Net cost usually neutral or slightly better if steady-state is maintained. The danger is burst-driven scale-ups.
[04:16] Rita: Burst-driven scale-ups are our fear. We have a strong constraint around monthly cost variability.
[04:21] Maya: Two mitigations: enable a short burst-capacity policy that allows limited bursting without new replica provisioning, and configure a conservative autoscaler cool-down so ephemeral spikes don't spin up new pods. We'll put recommended numbers in the runbook.
[04:35] Priya: Good — can you also explain fallback to quantized model? We saw in an earlier test you suggested a smaller quantized variant for tail handling.
[04:44] Devon: Sure — fallback is a policy: if queue depth or p99 crosses a threshold we route new requests to a smaller int8 quantized model (compat variant) that maintains functional parity for many prompts but with ~30–40% lower latency and cost per token. It's best for non-critical long-form jobs; we can selectively route by tenant or route.
[05:03] Priya: Are there any quality regressions we've observed in your A/B?
[05:08] Devon: Minimal for summarization tasks; we've added a guardrail: run a lightweight similarity check on the first chunk and if it drops below threshold, we can requeue on the full model asynchronously. But that adds complexity.
[05:22] Owen: Requeue async — will that create surprise UX?
[05:25] Devon: Should be fine for background jobs, not for synchronous UX. We'll mark synchronous auth flows as non-fallback.
[05:33] Samir: On the observed jitter, I want to point out one cause we saw: your traffic's long-flow bursts are correlated across tenants — simultaneous long calls from multiple tenants are causing overlap and large batches which cause memory pressure and intermittent GC-like stalls in the runtime.
[05:50] Priya: How can we avoid memory pressure? We can change client batching at our side, but that is expensive product work.
[05:55] Samir: We can mitigate on the Redwood side: enforce per-tenant concurrency caps, enforce max batch token budget (not just count), and ensure KV cache affinity by session. The cache affinity reduces cross-tenant eviction.
[06:12] Rita: Session affinity sounds promising; does it require sticky sessions?
[06:15] Devon: Minimal sticky routing — a token-level hash that keeps a session mapped to a replica for the life of a long flow. It increases cache warm rates significantly for your long-form summaries.
[06:25] Priya: But won't sticky routing reduce pooling efficiency?
[06:28] Samir: Slightly, yes, but for your workload the net effect is lower p99 because warmed caches avoid reloads; throughput impact is minor. We'll show numbers in the bench.
[06:38] Jon: Quick question on metrics — can you instrument per-replica cold start rate and share traces? We need that for our SRE.
[06:46] Devon: Yes, action item — we'll export p95/p99 queue latencies per replica and the sample traces with KV events flagged.
[06:53] Maya: Also I'll share the throughput-playbook-v2.xlsx which maps knobs to expected delta.
[06:58] Owen: Excellent. Are we going to run the benchmark with traffic slices reflecting our real short/long split?
[07:04] Maya: Please send us the split. We need two slices: 1) auth/short (avg 40 tokens) and 2) long-note (avg 1,100 tokens), with target arrival patterns. Priya?
[07:11] Priya: We'll prepare and upload by tomorrow.
[07:14] Devon: For the bench run we'll test three configs: baseline (80 conc, max_batch 64, window 30ms), hybrid-routing (split routes with small-window route for short queries), and high-concurrency (95 conc, max_batch 48, window 20ms) with sticky affinity enabled.
[07:30] Rita: Will you include the fallback quantized run in the same test?
[07:33] Devon: Yes, we'll run a fourth experiment where 15% of requests are allowed to fall back to the quantized variant when queue depth > threshold.
[07:41] Priya: That 15% is arbitrary — can we set it per-route?
[07:45] Devon: Absolutely, per-route or per-tenant. We'll propose defaults and you can override.
[07:50] Owen: One more ops question: logs and traces retention, our compliance team asked for 90-day logs and audit trail of model rollouts.
[07:58] Maya: We support configurable retention. For Private customers you can export to your S3/GCP bucket; for hosted we can do 90-day retention as a paid add-on and we'll provide rollout audit logs. I'll attach the security matrix.
[08:09] Priya: Perfect.
[08:12] Samir: Quick note on autoscale cool-down: set it to 300s in the pilot so that short bursts don't spin up new replicas; combine with burst-capacity to absorb short spikes.
[08:22] Priya: Sounds good.
[08:24] Devon: Last operational thing — we'll instrument a circuit-breaker that rejects requests when queue latency exceeds 1.5x SLO and route to fallback or return 429 depending on route policies.
[08:37] Rita: We'll prefer fallback for non-interactive jobs and 429 for interactive where we want to fail fast.
[08:41] Maya: Okay time check — ten minutes left. Let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:47] Devon: I'll run the three/four bench configs tomorrow night and share raw traces + summary by Thursday morning.
[08:53] Priya: We'll provide the traffic slices + example traces by tomorrow.
[08:57] Samir: I'll push a config to the pilot cluster with sticky routing and a per-tenant concurrency cap for testing, and validate memory pressure improvements.
[09:06] Maya: I'll send security docs and the throughput playbook; also schedule the KV cache debugging session.
[09:12] Jon: Thanks everyone, this was productive.
[09:15] Rita: Thanks — that's all from us.
[09:18] Maya: Great, we'll follow up with the timeline and invite for the debugging session.

End of transcript.
